cards.explanation: The answer is miserable comforters. Job says, "I have heard many things like these; miserable comforters are you all." (Job 16:2) Eliphaz, one of his three friends (Job 2:11), had just finished his speech (Job 15). I bet Job was hoping for a hug and got a lecture instead.

The answer is True. Job tells his friends, "I could also speak like you if you were in my place; I could heap up words against you and shake my head at you." (Job 16:4) He knows how to talk like that. The next verse says what he'd do instead.

The answer is to encourage them. Job says, "But I would encourage you with my mouth, and the consolation of my lips would bring relief." (Job 16:5) He knows what real comfort sounds like, and it doesn't sound like a lecture. Honestly, that's a good rule for anybody visiting a hurting friend.
The answer is all his family. Job says, "Surely He has now exhausted me; You have devastated all my family." (Job 16:7) That's the weight he's carrying. I think this one hurts.

The answer is True. Job says, "God has delivered me to unjust men; He has thrown me to the clutches of the wicked." (Job 16:11) These are Job's own words about how it feels to him. A heavy verse, so we just let it sit and read it plainly.
The word is target. Job says, "He has set me up as His target…" (Job 16:12) Right after, he talks about archers surrounding him (Job 16:13). That's how it feels to Job, and he says it plainly.

Violence goes in the first blank, and pure goes in the second. Job says, "…yet my hands are free of violence and my prayer is pure." (Job 16:17) He's standing by his innocence even while he's hurting. That takes backbone. Even with all that sorrow, he keeps praying, and I respect that.

The answer is False. Job says, "O earth, do not cover my blood; may my cry for help never be laid to rest." (Job 16:18) He asks for the opposite: no covering of his blood, and no resting for his cry for help.

The answer is in heaven. Job says, "Even now my witness is in heaven, and my advocate is on high." (Job 16:19) In the middle of all that pain, he looks up. I think that's a bright spot in a dark chapter.

The answer is True. Job says, "Oh, that a man might plead with God as he pleads with his neighbor!" (Job 16:21) He wishes a man could plead with God the way he would plead with his neighbor. It's a wish, and he says it out loud.

The answer is that he will go the way of no return. Job says, "For when only a few years are past I will go the way of no return." (Job 16:22) He's looking at the end of his life, and he doesn't sugarcoat it. This part is heavy, so we just let it be heavy.

The answer is mockers. Job says, "Surely mockers surround me, and my eyes must gaze at their rebellion." (Job 17:2) He's got the grave ahead and mockers all around. That's a rough view from where he's sitting.
The answer is False. Job says, "You have closed their minds to understanding; therefore You will not exalt them." (Job 17:4) Exalted is exactly what Job says they won't be.
The word is face. Job says, "He has made me a byword among the people, a man in whose face they spit." (Job 17:6) That's about as disrespectful as it gets. Job doesn't hide how bad it feels.

The answer is that they are appalled. Job says, "The upright are appalled at this, and the innocent are stirred against the godless." (Job 17:8) The upright look at what's happening and they're shocked. Job says it plainly, so we take it plainly.

The word is stronger. Job says, "Yet a righteous one holds to his way, and the one with clean hands grows stronger." (Job 17:9) Even in the middle of all this pain, Job says that. That's a man holding on, friends.

The answer is False. Job tells his friends, "But come back and try again, all of you. For I will not find a wise man among you." (Job 17:10) He doesn't expect to find a wise man in the bunch. That's him being honest.

The question is where is my hope. Job asks, "…where then is my hope? Who can see any hope for me?" (Job 17:15) He's picturing Sheol as his home, and the question just hangs there. It's a heavy moment, and the text lets it stay heavy.
The answer is True. Job ends with, "Will it go down to the gates of Sheol? Will we go down together into the dust?" (Job 17:16) It's a question, not an answer. And the story keeps going after it.
